title: From a prompt to numbers
text: Why does an AI assistant pause before its answer starts appearing, and why does the answer then arrive a little at a time? Those two moments reflect different kinds of work. Let’s follow a simple request through a language model and see where the time goes. We will use the sentence, the capital of Japan is, and watch how the system could continue it with Tokyo. This is an illustration of a typical causal transformer. Real token boundaries, numerical values and serving systems vary. The journey has four parts. First, text becomes tokens. Next, prefill processes the prompt. Then decode generates a continuation. Finally, the service sends the result back to the application. Before the model runs, the service may authenticate the request, apply limits and place it in a queue. A scheduler decides when the available hardware can handle it. That waiting time matters, because the delay you experience is not all model computation. Now look at the sentence. A tokenizer converts its text into identifiers drawn from a fixed vocabulary. A token might be a word, a fragment of a word, punctuation or another unit. Five words do not necessarily mean five tokens. For our diagram, we will use five simplified pieces so the computation stays readable. Each identifier selects a learned embedding, which is a vector of numbers. Position information also enters the model, so the same pieces in a different order can lead to a different result. The vectors pass through a stack of transformer blocks. Within a block, attention brings information from allowed positions together, and a feedforward network transforms the representation. Residual paths and normalization help those transformations work together. In a causal model, a position cannot look ahead to future tokens. It can use itself and earlier context. That restriction is what lets the model generate from left to right. During prefill, many prompt positions are processed in parallel within each layer, but the layers still depend on one another. At the top, the final prompt position provides the representation used to score the first new token. Earlier positions were useful: they supplied context for that final position through the attention computation. The system has now turned your text into a numerical state from which it can choose a continuation.

title: How one token becomes an answer
text: The final representation is not a tiny sentence with a city name written inside it. It is a learned pattern of numerical features. An output projection converts that pattern into one score for each token in the vocabulary. Those raw scores are called logits. In our example, the token that begins Tokyo might receive a high score, while unrelated continuations receive lower ones. The bars on screen are illustrative, not measurements from a real model run. Softmax converts the scores into a probability distribution. A decoding rule then selects a token. Greedy decoding chooses the highest-scoring option. Sampling can choose among several plausible options, and settings such as temperature reshape that distribution. Lower temperature usually concentrates probability on stronger candidates; higher temperature spreads it more widely. Neither setting turns likelihood into a guarantee of factual correctness. Once a token is chosen, it becomes part of the sequence. The model uses that extended sequence to predict another token, perhaps punctuation in this example, and the process repeats until a stopping condition is reached. This is autoregressive generation. The system is not usually writing the whole final answer in a single ordinary decoding step. To understand how it avoids repeating all its earlier work, we need to look inside attention. At a given layer, learned projections create queries, keys and values from the representations. One useful intuition is that a query describes what a position is looking for, a key helps determine how relevant another position is, and a value carries information that can be combined. These are all vectors, not literal questions or dictionary entries. The model compares a query with the allowed keys, scales the scores and applies a mask. A softmax turns the resulting scores into attention weights. Those weights form a mixture of the values. Different heads can learn different relationships, and the combined result continues through the block. Our arrows emphasize a few connections to make the idea visible, but actual attention is distributed across numerical representations. It is also only one part of a transformer block. The feedforward network, residual connections and normalization contribute to the output. All of these transformations use parameters learned during training. During a normal inference request, the model uses those parameters; it is not automatically updating its weights from this one conversation. What changes as the answer grows is the sequence and the request’s temporary state.

title: The cache, prefill and decode
text: Here is the useful consequence of causal attention. Once an earlier token has been processed at a layer, appending a later token does not change that earlier token’s keys and values. So the system can retain them. That stored state is the key value cache, usually shortened to the K V cache. Each layer maintains the information needed for later attention computations. The cache is not a database of facts, and it is not the model’s permanent learned memory. It is working state associated with processed context. Without this reuse, a simple implementation could repeatedly recompute the previous sequence as it generates each new token. With the cache, a new token computes its own query, key and value, appends the new key and value, and attends to the relevant cached history. Past queries generally do not need to be retained for ordinary next-token decoding. Picture the computation as a grid. Columns represent token positions and rows represent layers. In prefill, the prompt columns enter together. At each layer, their representations are transformed and their keys and values are stored. The work advances through the layers until the final prompt position can produce the first new-token distribution. This stage often uses large matrix operations efficiently, especially with long prompts. It is commonly compute-heavy, although the actual bottleneck depends on the model, hardware and workload. After we select Tokyo, decode processes that new token through the layers while reusing the prompt’s cached state. The next token is selected, added to the sequence and processed in turn. For ordinary decoding, those successive steps depend on one another. You cannot compute a later sampled token before the earlier choice is known. That explains the difference between waiting for the answer to start and watching the answer grow. Time to first token includes queueing, request preparation, prefill and other service overheads. The interval between later tokens reflects the decoding and delivery path. A long prompt can therefore create a long initial wait even when the eventual output streams smoothly. A long requested answer can keep the accelerator busy for many sequential decoding steps. Both matter for user experience, but they are different measurements. When diagnosing a slow assistant, measure the initial wait and the subsequent output rate separately before choosing an optimization.

title: Why serving systems matter
text: Why can a very powerful accelerator still generate only a limited number of tokens each second? Computation is only part of the job. Parameters and cached state also have to move through memory. At small batch sizes, decoding dense models is often limited by memory bandwidth: moving the data can take longer than the arithmetic. As a scale illustration, eight billion parameters stored with two bytes per parameter occupy about sixteen billion bytes, before the cache and other runtime overheads. That is a storage estimate, not a promise about every model’s actual traffic or speed. Quantization can reduce the precision used for weights and sometimes other tensors, which changes memory requirements and may improve performance. It also requires quality checks and appropriate hardware support. Serving multiple requests together is another important technique. A batch lets hardware reuse work on shared model weights across several sequences. Each request still needs its own context state and correct isolation. With continuous batching, the scheduler can admit new requests as others finish instead of waiting for an entire fixed batch to end. Larger batches may improve overall throughput, but user latency depends on scheduling and resource contention. The best batch is not simply the biggest one. The key value cache consumes memory too, and it usually grows with the number of stored tokens. Its size depends on architecture, attention heads, precision and implementation. Memory management techniques such as paged caches can help reduce waste and support more requests. Prefix caching can reuse computation for an eligible prompt prefix that has already been processed. Speculative decoding takes a different approach: a proposal mechanism suggests several tokens, and the target model verifies them. Speedup depends on how often the proposals are accepted and how expensive verification is. None of these techniques is a universal fix. Once generated tokens are converted back into text, the service streams chunks to the client. A chunk does not always correspond to exactly one token, and network buffering can affect what you see. The response finishes when a stop condition or output limit is reached. Now we can reconnect the whole picture. Tokenization prepares the input. Prefill processes its context and populates the cache. Decode extends the sequence while reusing that state. Scheduling, memory and streaming determine how efficiently the result reaches you. When an assistant feels slow, ask two questions: what delayed the first token, and what limited the tokens that followed? Those questions lead to much better engineering decisions than simply asking for a bigger model.
